meta.title: Who really said "Luke, I am your father"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Darth Vader never says "Luke." The real line is "No. I am your father" — a reply, not a sentence. Written by Lucas and Kasdan, not Brackett.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Luke, I am your father'?
meta.ogDescription: Vader never says "Luke." The actual line is "No. I am your father" — and the "No." is the part that matters. Here's the transcript.

answer.label: Not quite — the actual line is “No. I am your father.”
answer.authorDates: Screenplay credit, The Empire Strikes Back (1980) · story by George Lucas
answer.sourceLine: Darth Vader never says “Luke.” In The Empire Strikes Back (1980) the line is “No. I am your father” — and the “No.” is doing the work, because it contradicts Luke’s accusation that Vader killed his father. The popular version swaps that rebuttal for a name that is never spoken in the scene.
answer.confidenceText: The film and the moment are real; only the wording drifted.

source.heading: The actual exchange

docMeta.dd: Screenplay by Leigh Brackett & Lawrence Kasdan; story by George Lucas
Darth Vader (David Prowse; voiced by James Earl Jones) — a fictional character
The duel with Luke Skywalker, Cloud City

source.excerpt:
Vader: Obi-Wan never told you what happened to your father.
Luke: He told me enough. He told me you killed him.
Vader: No. I am your father.
trail: 1980 — the film. The Empire Strikes Back opens 21 May 1980. Wikiquote’s transcription ↗ records the Cloud City exchange as “No. I am your father” — the earliest and only place the line is actually spoken.

Written in secret, not by one hand. Brackett’s first draft had no such twist and she died in March 1978 ↗; Lucas wrote the next draft himself ↗ and Kasdan polished the dialogue. On set the secret held: only Kershner, Lucas and Hamill knew ↗.

No earlier source. The Glut novelization ↗ reached print on 12 April 1980, before the film — but it is “based on the screenplay,” so it is downstream of the script. There is no novel or play behind this line.
The misquote is documented, not disputed. Lucasfilm ↗ and ACMI ↗ both state plainly that “Luke, I am your father” is not the line.
source.excerptNote: Quoted from Wikiquote’s transcription ↗. Luke’s middle line is included because it is what the “No.” answers — the reason the real wording cannot survive being quoted alone.

source.rightsNote: The Empire Strikes Back was released in 1980 — half a century after the 1930 US public-domain cutoff — so the film and its screenplay are firmly in copyright. Screenwriting is work-for-hire: the rights sit with the studio, Lucasfilm Ltd. ↗, not with Brackett’s estate or Kasdan personally. The brief exchange above is quoted for identification and correction of a widely repeated misquotation.

author.name: Leigh Brackett & Lawrence Kasdan
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: Screenwriters, The Empire Strikes Back (1980) · story by George Lucas
author.bio: The film’s screenplay is credited to Leigh Brackett (1915–1978), the science-fiction novelist and Howard Hawks veteran nicknamed “the Queen of Space Opera,” and Lawrence Kasdan (b. 1949), who went on to write Raiders of the Lost Ark and direct The Big Chill. The credit is shared, but not evenly: Brackett delivered a first draft shortly before her death in March 1978 and, per Wikipedia, was credited “in tribute despite not being involved in the final film.” Lucas, dissatisfied, wrote the next draft himself — the one that established the major plot twists — and Kasdan was then hired to polish the dialogue. This line therefore traces to Lucas’s draft and Kasdan’s dialogue work, not to Brackett’s; it is an authorship no single name honestly covers.

copyAttribution: "No. I am your father." — Darth Vader (voiced by James Earl Jones) in The Empire Strikes Back (1980), screenplay by Leigh Brackett and Lawrence Kasdan, story by George Lucas. The popular "Luke, I am your father" is never spoken in the film.

misattribution.heading: What the retelling changed
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here — the film is right, the villain is right, the moment is right. Three smaller things went wrong, and only one of them is the famous one.

items.why: The name is an addition and the “No.” is a deletion. Wikiquote’s transcription ↗ has Vader say “No. I am your father” — contradicting Luke, who has just said Vader killed his father. Strip the “No.” and you lose the fact that the line is a rebuttal. Lucasfilm itself gives the line as “No, I am your father” ↗.

Prowse wore the suit but never spoke these words: he “was told nothing, and spoke placeholder dialogue” ↗. The voice everyone quotes is James Earl Jones, dubbed in later. Neither man wrote it, and neither is the line’s author.

Lucas has the story credit and, per Wikipedia ↗, wrote the draft that established the twist — but the screenplay credit reads Brackett and Kasdan, and Kasdan polished the dialogue. Conversely, crediting Brackett overshoots too: she died in March 1978 and was credited “in tribute despite not being involved in the final film” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The moment is exactly as remembered; the sentence is not. Vader says “No. I am your father” ↗ — answering an accusation, not announcing himself to a name.

context.heading: Why this one drifted
lead: The misremembered version is arguably the better standalone sentence — and that is exactly why it spread. Lifted out of the scene, “No. I am your father” is a non-sequitur: no to what? The line only parses as a reply, because Luke has just said Vader killed his father. To quote it on its own, people unconsciously repaired it, swapping the dangling rebuttal for the name of the person being addressed. The misquote is a self-contained sentence; the real line is half of a two-person exchange.

The scene was also built to be hidden, which left the words unusually free to wander. David Prowse, inside the Vader suit, was never given the real dialogue — he spoke placeholder lines, and only Lucas, director Irvin Kershner and Mark Hamill knew the twist. James Earl Jones’s voice was laid in afterwards. The line that lodged in the culture was never performed on set at all.
detailsBody: A curiosity that bears on the “where did it come from” question: Donald F. Glut’s novelization, published by Del Rey on 12 April 1980, reached readers before the film opened on 21 May 1980 — so the revelation was in print before any audience saw it. That does not make the book the line’s origin. The novelization is expressly “based on the screenplay… by Leigh Brackett and Lawrence Kasdan from story by George Lucas” — it is downstream of the script, not upstream of it. Unlike Gone with the Wind, where the film sharpened a line already in Mitchell’s novel, here there is no earlier novel or play to credit.
context.pull: The misquote is a sentence. The real line is an answer.
